skills.name: Factorise quadratic trinomials x² + bx + c

note.text:
To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Then x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q).
• x² + 7x + 12: 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7, so (x + 3)(x + 4).
• x² − 2x − 15: −5 × 3 = −15 and −5 + 3 = −2, so (x − 5)(x + 3).
Signs: if c is positive, both numbers have the sign of b. If c is negative, the numbers have opposite signs and the larger one has the sign of b.
Check by expanding: the middle term must come back.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to factorise any trinomial x² + bx + c with whole numbers, choosing the signs correctly.
Builds on: Lesson {2} (expanding (x + p)(x + q)) and Lesson {3} (factorising by grouping).
Leads to: Lesson {6} (trinomials with a number in front of x²) and solving quadratic equations by factorisation.

sections.heading: Product and sum
sections.text:
Expand {lin2(1, 3, 1, 4)}: x² + {mono(4, 'x')} + {mono(3, 'x')} + {12} = {quad(1, 7, 12)}.
The two numbers {3} and {4} multiply to give {12} and add to give {7}. So to factorise {quad(1, 7, 12)}, ask: which two numbers multiply to {12} and add to {7}?
List the factor pairs of {12}: {1} × {12}, {2} × {6}, {3} × {4}. Only {3} and {4} add to {7}.
Then {quad(1, 7, 12)} = {lin2(1, 3, 1, 4)}.

sections.heading: Getting the signs right
sections.text:
• c positive, b positive: both numbers positive. {quad(1, 8, 15)} = {lin2(1, 3, 1, 5)}.
• c positive, b negative: both negative. {quad(1, -8, 15)} = {lin2(1, -3, 1, -5)}.
• c negative: one positive, one negative. The larger has the sign of b. {quad(1, -2, -15)} = {lin2(1, -5, 1, 3)}.
Always expand to check. Common factors come out first: {quad(2, 14, 24)} = {2}({quad(1, 7, 12)}).

key_words.meaning: an expression with three terms, such as {quad(1, 5, 6)}
with x² as the highest power of x
two whole numbers that multiply to a given number

mistake.why: {5} + {br(-3)} = {2}, but the middle term is {mono(-2, 'x')}. The larger number takes the sign of b: {-5} and {3}.

steps: Look for two numbers with product {p * q} and sum {p + q}.
The product is negative, so the numbers have opposite signs.
Pairs with product {p * q}: … {p} and {q} add to {p + q}.
Check: {lin2(1, p, 1, q)} = {quad(1, p + q, p * q)}.

cards.idea: For x² + bx + c, look for two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.
If c is positive and b is negative, both numbers are negative.
If c is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs; the larger one has the sign of b.

misconceptions.explain: Expand it: the middle term would be {mono(-(p + q), 'x')}. Swap the signs.
{br(-p)} × {br(q)} = {-p * q}: the product would be positive.
{p} × {br(-q)} = {-p * q}: the product would be positive.

solution: The product {p * q} is negative: the numbers have opposite signs.

misconceptions.explain: The numbers in the brackets must multiply to {p * q} and add to {p + q}. {p + q} and {p * q} do not.
{br(-p)} + {br(-q)} = {-p - q}. The middle term is +{p + q}x, so both numbers are positive.

solution: Two numbers with product {p * q} and sum {p + q}: {p} and {q}.

misconceptions.explain: {lin2(1, p, 1, q)} expands to {quad(1, p + q, p * q)}: the middle sign is wrong.
One plus and one minus give a negative product, {-p * q}. Here the product is +{p * q}.

solution: The product +{p * q} is positive and the sum {-(p + q)} is negative: both numbers are negative.

misconceptions.explain: Expand it: the middle term would be {mono(-(p + q), 'x')}. Swap the signs.
{br(-p)} × {br(q)} = {-p * q}: the product would be positive.
{p} × {br(-q)} = {-p * q}: the product would be positive.

solution: The product {p * q} is negative: the numbers have opposite signs.

questions.prompt: {quad(1, p + q, p * q)} = (x + {br(p)})(x + k). What is k?

misconceptions.explain: k is not the middle coefficient. The two numbers multiply to {p * q}: k = {q}.

solution: The two numbers multiply to {p * q}: {p} × k = {p * q}, so k = {q}.

questions.prompt: Ayuk factorised {quad(1, p + q, p * q)} as {lin2(1, -p, 1, -q)}. What went wrong?
questions.correct: The signs are swapped: the answer is {lin2(1, p, 1, q)}

distractors.text: The numbers should be {p * q} and {1}

misconceptions.explain: Expand it: Ayuk's brackets give {mono(-(p + q), 'x')}, not {mono(p + q, 'x')}.
It does factorise: {p} and {q} multiply to {p * q} and add to {p + q}.

solution: Expand Ayuk's answer: {lin2(1, -p, 1, -q)} = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)}.
The middle term has the wrong sign. The right factorisation is {lin2(1, p, 1, q)}.
